newsitem.title: UK: London dealers wary ahead of U.S. rate decision.
newsitem.headline: London dealers wary ahead of U.S. rate decision.

text.p: Commodity dealers were wary on Tuesday ahead of a meeting of the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) which was widely expected to recommend raising interest rates.
"The expectations are for a modest rise. I think it's been built into the price so we're not exactly waiting with bated breath," a gold bullion dealer said.
Gold and silver popped higher on a spate of short covering, but dealers said the market was wary ahead of the FOMC meeting.
Bullion fixed at $382.30 an ounce, versus $381.00 on Monday afternoon. Silver also edged up slightly after hitting an 18-month low of $4.9450 last week.
Several dealers said a quarter-point rise in U.S. rates had already been priced into the market.
The test for gold would be how it responded to Wall Street's reaction to a rate rise. Speculative investment funds were likely to start selling if the price crept higher.
"They'll be quite happy to sell silver at $5.00 and gold at $383.50-$384.00," a dealer said.
On the London Metal Exchange (LME), copper broke above the key $1,900 level as traders bought cash metal in response to the exchange's warehouses stocks falling more than forecast.
Most of the other base metals ticked higher in sympathy.
Three months copper firmed about $40 a tonne after stocks fell by 8,825 tonnes, nearly 6,000 tonnes more than expected.
Many analysts had been expecting copper to remain under pressure after slipping under $1,900 in late trading on Friday and losing ground again on Monday.
Aluminium edged up around $8.00 from Monday's depressed closing levels to about $1,400.
"I've seen some good consumer buying, but that doesn't mean it won't go lower," a floor trader said.
Robusta coffee futures recovered from over two-year lows of $1,475 a tonne on Monday to just over $1,500.
"It's pretty much an unexpected little rally. "There's no special news," said one trader.
Cocoa was quiet and ended off five pounds at 984. Sugar lost ground when New York selling overwhelmed earlier support. The December contract fell $0.80 to $329.50 by 1620 GMT.
European grains prices were mostly lower led by wheat prices after rising in response to higher French prices last week.
Barley prices, especially in Britain, weakened on expectations that a recent 1.4 million tonne order from Saudi Arabia would be met largely from France.
U.S. soybean futures were lower also in response to improved growing conditions and the weakness spilled over to other grains futures in the Chicago and Kansas City markets.
